newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria parliament overturns investment law veto.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria parliament overturns investment law veto.

text.p: Bulgaria's Socialist-dominated parliament on Friday overturned President Zhelyu Zhelev's veto on amendments to the foreign investment law, state radio said.

On November 28, parliament approved amendments introducing a minimum $50,000 foreign investment registration threshold, and denying profit repatriation and other investment incentives to some 6,800 smaller joint-venture companies.
Zhelev vetoed the amendments last week, saying they would deter new investment and were contrary to the national interest.
The chairman of the parliamentary budget committee, Kiril Zhelev, said the president's motives for vetoing the law were political rather than economic.

Supporters of the amendments say they extended some tax benefits in a bid to speed up privatisation, exempting non-fiscal foreign investments like machines and equipment, patent rights, licences, trademarks, technologies and know-how from Value Added Tax, customs duties and other taxes.

The president criticised an amendment which set a 10-year limit after registration for protection of foreign investments against possible legislative curbs that might come into force during that period. Until now, foreign investors could rely on this preferential legislative treatment indefinitely.

Zhelev also criticised an amendment banning foreign investors from farmland ownership irrespective of their stake in a joint venture. Until now the ban had applied only for foreign investors holding a stake of more than 50 percent.
The director of Bulgaria's foreign investment agency, Daniela Bobeva, resigned after parliament approved the amendments.

Parliament is dominated by the Bulgarian Socialist Party, while Zhelev is supported by the anti-communist opposition Union of Democratic Forces. Opposition parliamentary groups could appeal to the constitutional court as a last resort.

Bulgaria has the lowest level of foreign investment among its ex-communist neighbours. The Balkan country of 8.4 million people has attracted around $800 million in investments from abroad since 1990.
